{"outside":"Six-sided prisms with pointed ends, single or in clusters; doubly terminated crystals are rare. Scepters are a larger crystal on the end of a smaller one; a Japan-law twin is two flat crystals joined at about 84 degrees (USFS Crystal Park brochure 2023). Surface pockets often hold frost-damaged plates (Dillhoff & George 2016 p.502).","colour":"Clear, milky (\"finely dissembled gas bubbles\"), smoky grey to black, and amethyst purple (USFS 2023). Smoky colour is aluminium in the quartz plus natural radiation; amethyst is iron plus radiation (Fritsch & Rossman 1988). Hansen Creek and other surface amethyst is often pale (Dillhoff & George 2016 p.516).","checks":"Look for the pocket signs: \"reddish brown zones in the light colored granite\" that trace old veins to \"'pockets' of crystals\" (USFS 2023); clay- or sericite-lined pockets and limonite-stained rock (USGS OF 75-3; Dillhoff & George); aplite and pegmatite dikes near cavities (Williams et al. 2004). Dig with hand tools and chopsticks.","not_it":"Quartz \"crystals\" in a map's rock description are grains in the rock, not collectible points. Geode linings belong to the agate card.","care":"Clear quartz can be washed in a warm bleach solution; amethyst \"may shatter in hot water or lose their purple color at high temperatures\" (USFS 2023), and heat takes the smoky colour out too (Fritsch & Rossman 1988). Orange iron stain comes off in citric or oxalic acid (Rock & Gem 2024)."}
